Warrington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Cheshire and the Mersey corridor
s1loc: Warrington anchors a busy visitor economy between Manchester and Liverpool, with Gulliver's World drawing families to its themed zones at Old Hall and the RAF Burtonwood Heritage Centre marking what was once Europe's largest wartime airfield. Warrington Museum and Art Gallery, one of the oldest municipal museums in the country, and the landmark Golden Square Shopping Centre keep the town centre busy with day-trippers across the year.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the water and green spaces, from Sankey Valley Park and its canal towpaths to Walton Hall and Gardens with its heritage and play areas. Bank Quay, the Mersey waterfront and watersports on local meres give operators steady seasonal work, while indoor activity venues, soft-play sites and the Orford Jubilee leisure hub keep the schedule full through the colder months.

Heritage and culture run deep across Warrington, from the Grade I Warrington Town Hall and its golden gates to the historic Bridge Street quarter and the Pyramid and Parr Hall arts venues. Stockton Heath and Lymm bring riverside charm and festival crowds, while the town's rugby league heritage at the Halliwell Jones Stadium adds match-day visitors and stadium tours to the calendar.

Underpinning it all is a strong hotel and conference base around Birchwood, Centre Park and the M6 and M62 junctions, with tour operators and coach firms running day trips out to Cheshire and the Lake District. Warrington Bank Quay and Central stations sit on the West Coast Main Line, bringing visitors in from London, Glasgow and the wider North West for the area's attractions and shopping.

Slough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Berkshire
s1loc: Slough sits at the gateway to one of the busiest visitor corners of Berkshire, minutes from the LEGOLAND Windsor Resort with its fifty-plus rides and the royal draws of Windsor Castle just down the road. Herschel Park, a restored Victorian park and Local Nature Reserve named for the astronomer William Herschel, and the redeveloped Queensmere centre give the town its own everyday footfall alongside the regional attractions.

The leisure and activity layer leans heavily on the surrounding countryside, with Black Park Country Park and its lake and woodland trails sitting beside Pinewood Studios, and Langley Park offering wide open spaces and the famous Rhododendron Walk. Salt Hill Park, the Arbour Park sports ground and indoor activity and trampoline venues keep families and operators busy through the seasons, well beyond the summer peak.

Heritage and culture cluster around the historic core and nearby landmarks, from the Curve cultural centre and library to St Mary's Church and Upton Court Park. Just across the borough boundary the heritage of Stoke Poges, with the churchyard that inspired Gray's Elegy, and Eton's historic high street and college add culture-rich day-trip options to the events and festival calendar.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel and serviced-apartment base built around the Slough Trading Estate, Heathrow and the Thames Valley business corridor, with tour operators running airport and London transfers and Windsor day trips. Slough station and the new Elizabeth line bring visitors straight in from central London, while the M4 and M40 feed coach traffic to LEGOLAND and Windsor.

Huddersfield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Kirklees Pennines
s1loc: Huddersfield draws visitors to one of the finest hilltop landmarks in Yorkshire, the Grade II Victoria Tower on Castle Hill, an ancient monument with a hillfort and motte history stretching back four thousand years. The town's magnificent Victorian railway station frontage on St George's Square, the Tolson Memorial Museum in Ravensknowle Park and the surrounding Pennine moors give the visitor economy a strong heritage and scenic core.

The leisure and activity layer spreads out into spectacular countryside, from the reservoirs and trails of the Holme Valley to the rugged moorland above Marsden and the Standedge Tunnel and Visitor Centre on the Huddersfield Narrow Canal. Beaumont Park, Greenhead Park and indoor activity, climbing and trampoline venues across the town keep families and outdoor operators working hard right through the year.

Heritage and culture run strong in Huddersfield, with the Lawrence Batley Theatre in a converted Methodist chapel programming drama, dance and comedy, and the University and its galleries adding to the mix. The historic Byram Arcade, the Marsden Jazz Festival and the wider Kirklees events calendar bring crowds to the town centre, while nearby Holmfirth carries its own famous screen and festival heritage.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base across the town and the surrounding valleys, with walking and cycling guides leading visitors onto the moors and the Pennine routes. Huddersfield station sits on the trans-Pennine line between Manchester and Leeds, and the M62 brings day-trippers and coach tours in from both cities for the area's heritage and countryside draws.

Telford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Shropshire
s1loc: Telford sits at the heart of the Ironbridge Gorge World Heritage Site, where the world's first iron bridge crossed the River Severn in 1779 and the Ironbridge Gorge Museum Trust now runs ten museums including Blists Hill Victorian Town and Coalport China. The nearby RAF Museum Cosford, with its vast aircraft collection, gives the town two visitor draws of genuine national standing pulling crowds across the year.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the huge Telford Town Park, one of the largest urban parks in the country, sitting beside Southwater with its lake, plaza and the Telford Shopping Centre. Wonderland, the fairytale-themed adventure park set in woodland, alongside indoor soft-play, climbing and watersports venues across the borough, keeps family operators and activity centres busy through every season.

Heritage and culture run beyond the Gorge too, from the historic Oakengates and Dawley districts and the Sunday flea market to Hadley and Madeley and the Telford Theatre programme. The town's New Town origins sit alongside genuinely old quarters, and the festival and events calendar at Southwater and the Town Park brings crowds to outdoor concerts and seasonal markets throughout the year.

Underpinning it all is a strong hotel and conference base around the International Centre and the M54 corridor, with tour operators running Ironbridge and Shropshire Hills day trips and coach tours to Cosford. Telford Central station links to Birmingham and Shrewsbury, and the motorway brings visitors and coaches in from the West Midlands for the World Heritage attractions and the surrounding countryside.

Newport.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Gwent and the Usk valley
s1loc: Newport's marquee landmark is the Grade I Transporter Bridge of 1906, one of the very few working transporter bridges left in the world, spanning the River Usk beside the medieval Newport Castle. The National Trust's Tredegar House, a Charles II mansion set in ninety acres of parkland and ancestral home of the Morgan family for five centuries, gives the city a visitor draw of genuine heritage weight.

The leisure and activity layer reaches out to the coast and the hills, with the RSPB Newport Wetlands and its reedbeds, lagoons and birdlife on the Severn Estuary, and the Fourteen Locks Canal Centre on the Monmouthshire and Brecon Canal. Belle Vue Park, the riverfront and watersports on the Usk, plus indoor activity and climbing venues, keep operators and families busy across the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep in and around the city, above all at Caerleon, one of only three permanent Roman legionary fortresses in Britain, with its amphitheatre, baths and barracks linked in legend to King Arthur's court. The Riverfront arts centre and theatre, the regenerated Friars Walk quarter and Newport's festival calendar add a strong cultural draw to the year-round events programme.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base across the city and the Celtic Manor Resort, a major conference and golf venue that hosted the Ryder Cup and a NATO summit. Newport station sits on the South Wales Main Line between Cardiff and Bristol, and Rodney Parade brings rugby and football match-day crowds, with the M4 feeding coach tours to the area's Roman and industrial heritage.

Oxford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Oxfordshire
s1loc: Oxford runs one of the most visited heritage economies in the country, built around the dreaming spires of its historic colleges, the Radcliffe Camera and Bodleian Library, and the great free museums of the Ashmolean and the Pitt Rivers. Christ Church, with its hall famous from Harry Potter, and the climb up the University Church of St Mary the Virgin tower draw millions of visitors to the city centre across the year.

The leisure and activity layer flows along the rivers, with punting on the Cherwell and the Isis from the Magdalen Bridge and Folly Bridge boathouses, and walks through the University Parks and Christ Church Meadow. Port Meadow, the open-air pool at Hinksey, indoor climbing and activity venues and the green spaces of Headington keep families and outdoor operators working through every season.

Heritage and culture saturate the city, from the Sheldonian Theatre and the Oxford Playhouse to the Bridge of Sighs at Hertford College and the covered Oxford Covered Market. The Story Museum, the New Theatre and a packed festival calendar, alongside Jericho and the historic streets of the centre, bring crowds to performances, exhibitions and seasonal events right across the year.

Underpinning it all is one of the deepest hotel, college-stay and guest-house bases outside London, with walking-tour guides and open-top bus operators leading visitors round the colleges. Oxford and Oxford Parkway stations link to London and Birmingham, Bicester Village pulls international shoppers, and the A34 and M40 bring coach tours in for the city's museums, colleges and surrounding countryside.

Poole.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Dorset coast
s1loc: Poole is built around one of the largest natural harbours in the world, with the historic Old Town quay, the Poole Museum and the boat trips out to National Trust Brownsea Island, home of the red squirrel and the birthplace of Scouting. The exclusive Sandbanks peninsula, its golden Blue Flag beaches and the chain ferry to Studland anchor a visitor economy that runs hard through the warmer months.

The leisure and activity layer is dominated by the water, from sailing, windsurfing and paddleboarding across Poole Harbour to the watersports schools and boat hire at Baiter and Hamworthy. Poole Park with its boating lake, Upton Country Park and indoor activity, climbing and play venues across the town give families and activity operators a packed programme that stretches well beyond the summer season.

Heritage and culture run through the Old Town's historic streets, the Guildhall and Scaplen's Court, with the Lighthouse arts centre, the largest in the South West, programming theatre, music and dance. The quayside Cockle Trail, seafood festivals and a busy events calendar of regattas and markets bring crowds to the harbour, while nearby Wimborne and Corfe Castle add day-trip heritage draws.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel, holiday-park and self-catering base across Poole, Sandbanks and the wider conurbation, with boat operators, fishing charters and guides working the harbour and the Jurassic Coast. Poole's cross-Channel ferry port links to France and the Channel Islands, the railway runs to Bournemouth and London Waterloo, and the resort coast keeps the seasonal trade busy.
